nodes.detail: Advisory body set up June 2004 under Sonia Gandhi (chair) to advise UPA government on policy. Members: civil society activists, intellectuals (Aruna Roy, Jean Drèze etc.). Drove RTI Act, NREGA, Forest Rights Act, Food Security Act. Disbanded 2014.

nodes.label: Sachar Committee (2005-06)
nodes.detail: High-level committee headed by Justice Rajindar Sachar to study social, economic and educational status of Muslims in India. Report submitted 17 November 2006. Found Muslims worse off than SCs/STs on many indicators. Drove Ministry of Minority Affairs and 15-Point Programme for Welfare of Minorities.

nodes.label: Ministry of Minority Affairs (2006)
nodes.detail: Created 29 January 2006 as separate ministry (earlier part of Ministry of Social Justice). Nodal ministry for 6 notified minority communities (Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis, Jains added 2014). Implements Pre-Matric/Post-Matric scholarships, Maulana Azad Foundation, Waqf matters.

nodes.label: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005
nodes.detail: Enacted September 2005, in effect 26 October 2006. Recognised physical, sexual, emotional, verbal, and economic abuse within shared households as domestic violence. Provided civil remedies (protection orders, residence orders, monetary relief). Applicable to any woman in domestic relationship regardless of marital status.

nodes.label: Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act 2005
nodes.detail: Amended Hindu Succession Act 1956. Made daughters equal coparceners in ancestral joint family property — same rights as sons by birth. Removed gender discrimination in Mitakshara coparcenary. Radical gender reform in inheritance law.

nodes.label: Right to Education Act 2009
nodes.detail: Enacted 4 August 2009, in force 1 April 2010. Operationalised Article 21A (86th Amendment 2002) guaranteeing free and compulsory education to all children aged 6-14. 25% reservation in private unaided schools for economically weaker sections. No detention till Class 8 (repealed 2019).

nodes.label: 27% OBC Reservation in Higher Education (2006)
nodes.detail: Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Admission) Act 2006. Introduced 27% OBC reservation in central universities and IITs/IIMs from 2007. Challenged in Ashoka Kumar Thakur case; Supreme Court upheld 2008 (with creamy layer exclusion).

nodes.label: Ashoka Kumar Thakur Case (2008)
nodes.detail: Supreme Court 5-judge bench (2008) upheld constitutional validity of 27% OBC reservation in central educational institutions under the 93rd Amendment (Article 15(5)). Applied creamy layer exclusion. Excluded minority educational institutions from reservation requirement.

nodes.label: Communal Violence (Prevention, Control and Rehabilitation of Victims) Bill
nodes.detail: Draft legislation introduced by UPA to prevent and control communal violence and rehabilitate victims. Multiple versions (2005, 2011, 2013) — targeted state failure in communal violence response. Opposed by states as encroachment on federal jurisdiction. Did not become law.

nodes.label: Indo-US Civilian Nuclear Agreement / 123 Agreement (2008)
nodes.detail: Civil nuclear cooperation agreement between India and US. Joint statement 18 July 2005 by Manmohan Singh-Bush. Text concluded July 2007. IAEA safeguards agreement August 2008. NSG waiver 6 September 2008. US 123 Agreement signed 10 October 2008. Ended India's nuclear isolation. Hyde Act and left withdrawal triggered trust vote July 2008.

nodes.label: NSG Waiver for India (6 September 2008)
nodes.detail: 48-member Nuclear Suppliers Group granted India unique 'clean waiver' on 6 September 2008 after US lobbying, despite India being non-NPT signatory. Enabled international civilian nuclear trade with India. Made possible the Indo-US Nuclear Deal operational.

nodes.label: UPA-I Trust Vote (July 2008)
nodes.detail: Confidence motion on Indo-US Nuclear Deal, 22 July 2008. Left Front withdrew support from UPA-I; Samajwadi Party switched to support. Manmohan Singh government survived 275-256. Cash-for-votes scandal — three BJP MPs displayed cash in Lok Sabha claiming bribery.

nodes.label: Clinton's India Visit (March 2000)
nodes.detail: US President Bill Clinton visited India 19-25 March 2000 — first US presidential visit since 1978 (Carter). Marked rapprochement after 1998 Pokhran sanctions. Declaration on 'Indo-US Relations: A Vision for the 21st Century'. Strategic relationship framework began.

nodes.label: Eighth Five-Year Plan (1992-97)
nodes.detail: First post-reform plan, 1992-97. Averaged 6.94% GDP growth (higher than Seventh Plan's 6%). Focus on rapid economic growth, infrastructure, energy, poverty alleviation. Savings rate rose to 23%+. Industrial growth peaked at 12.8% in 1995-96 on reform momentum.

nodes.label: Ninth Five-Year Plan (1997-2002)
nodes.detail: Growth target 6.5%, achieved 5.5% average. Slowdown due to East Asian crisis, oil shocks, 9/11 global slowdown. Focus on growth with social justice, food security, clean environment. Pokhran-II sanctions dampened first year.

nodes.label: Tenth Five-Year Plan (2002-07)
nodes.detail: Growth target 8%, achieved 7.6% average — at no point before had Indian economy sustained this growth over 5 years. Last 4 years averaged 8.6%; 2006-07 hit 9.4%. Services 68.6% contribution to growth. Proved India could target 9% for Eleventh Plan.

nodes.label: Eleventh Five-Year Plan (2007-12)
nodes.detail: Target 9% average GDP growth, inclusive growth theme. Ran through 2008 global financial crisis. Achieved 7.9% average. Bharat Nirman, NREGA scaling, flagship schemes. Tenure of Manmohan Singh-II.

nodes.label: Twelfth Five-Year Plan (2012-17) — Last Plan
nodes.detail: Final Five-Year Plan. Target 8% average growth, achieved ~6.7%. Theme: faster, sustainable and more inclusive growth. Ended with dissolution of Planning Commission (2014) and its replacement by NITI Aayog (2015). Post-2017 no formal five-year plan; NITI Aayog 3-year action agendas.

nodes.label: Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act (FRBMA) 2003
nodes.detail: Enacted August 2003, effective 5 July 2004. Committed central government to eliminate revenue deficit by March 2009 and reduce fiscal deficit to 3% of GDP. Parallel state FRBM laws. Suspended during 2008 crisis, 2020 pandemic. Amendments 2018 — fiscal deficit target of 3%/debt 40% of GDP.

nodes.label: Capital Issues (Control) Act Repeal 1992
nodes.detail: CICA 1947 repealed 29 May 1992. Ended government control over new issues and their pricing. Coincided with SEBI's transition from administrative body to statutory regulator. Opened primary capital markets to free pricing; triggered IPO boom.

nodes.label: MRTP Act Modifications (1991) / Repeal 2002
nodes.detail: Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act 1969. 1991 reforms removed asset threshold for MRTP registration and pre-entry scrutiny. Replaced by Competition Act 2002, which established Competition Commission of India (CCI, 2003, operational 2009). MRTP Act formally repealed 2009.

nodes.label: Competition Act 2002
nodes.detail: Enacted 2002, replaced MRTP Act. Prohibited anti-competitive agreements, abuse of dominance, regulated mergers/acquisitions. Established Competition Commission of India (CCI). Competition Appellate Tribunal (replaced by NCLAT 2017). Amendments 2007, 2023 (settlement framework).

nodes.label: Competition Commission of India (CCI)
nodes.detail: Regulatory body established under Competition Act 2002; became fully operational 20 May 2009. Headquartered in Delhi. Chair + 6 members. Enforces competition law, imposed fines on Google (2018), major cartels. Anti-trust regulator for Indian economy.

nodes.label: SEBI Made Statutory (SEBI Act 1992)
nodes.detail: Securities and Exchange Board of India Act 1992 gave SEBI (established 1988 as advisory body) statutory powers. Regulator for Indian capital markets. 3 objectives: protect investor interests, promote development, regulate securities markets. Headquartered Mumbai.

nodes.label: FDI Opening Post-1991
nodes.detail: Foreign Direct Investment liberalised 1991 Industrial Policy. Automatic approval up to 51% FDI in 34 high-priority sectors; further liberalised 1997, 2000 (automatic route 100% in most sectors). FDI grew from $129M in 1991-92 to $2.1bn in 1995-96, to $50+bn annually by 2010s. Defence 74% FDI (2020), insurance 74%.

nodes.label: Narasimham Committee I (1991)
nodes.detail: Committee on Financial System chaired by M. Narasimham, 1991. Recommendations: reduce SLR/CRR, phased deregulation of interest rates, capital adequacy norms (Basel), NPA classification, private banking entry, tribunal for NPA recovery. Basis for first-generation banking reforms.

nodes.label: Narasimham Committee II (1998)
nodes.detail: Committee on Banking Sector Reforms chaired by M. Narasimham, 1998. Recommendations: bank consolidation, capital adequacy to 10%, asset classification tightening, prudential norms, technology adoption. Set stage for second-generation banking reforms of 2000s including universal banking, private bank expansion.

nodes.label: Stock Market Expansion Post-1991
nodes.detail: Total market cap rose from 5% of GDP (1980) to 13% (1990) to 60% of GDP by end-1993. By 1995, Indian stock market had largest number of listed companies globally. Triggered by Capital Issues Control Act repeal 1992, FII access, SEBI empowerment, NSE establishment 1994.

nodes.label: National Stock Exchange (NSE, 1994)
nodes.detail: National Stock Exchange, incorporated 1992, commenced operations 1994. First fully electronic, screen-based exchange in India (breaking Bombay Stock Exchange monopoly). Introduced NIFTY 50 index 1996. Dominates equity and F&O trading. Derivatives launched 2000.

nodes.label: Musharraf Coup in Pakistan (12 October 1999)
nodes.detail: General Pervez Musharraf deposed PM Nawaz Sharif in bloodless military coup, 12 October 1999, three months after Kargil defeat. Sharif was attempting to remove Musharraf as Army Chief. Musharraf ruled 1999-2008, first as Chief Executive, then President (2001-08). Sharif exiled to Saudi Arabia.

nodes.label: NATO Bombing of Yugoslavia / Kosovo Crisis (1999)
nodes.detail: NATO-led bombing of Yugoslavia, March-June 1999, over Kosovo humanitarian crisis, without UN Security Council approval. India and Russia opposed as precedent for unilateral intervention. Marked shift towards R2P doctrine, deepened India-Russia multipolar vision alignment.

nodes.label: End of Punjab Militancy (early 1990s)
nodes.detail: Decade-long Khalistan insurgency in Punjab ended by mid-1990s after sustained counter-insurgency by KPS Gill-led Punjab Police (1991-95). Beant Singh became Congress CM 1992 (assassinated 1995 by LTTE-style suicide bomber). Normal politics restored 1997. Rajiv-Longowal Accord (1985) implemented partially.

nodes.label: Kashmir Insurgency Begins (1989)
nodes.detail: Armed insurgency in J&K from 1989 — JKLF, Hizbul Mujahideen. 1990 exodus of Kashmiri Pandits. Governor's rule under Jagmohan (Jan 1990). ~80,000 killed in subsequent years. Peaked 2001 (~4500 terror incidents). Declined post-2003 ceasefire. Article 370 abrogated 2019.

nodes.label: Kashmiri Pandits Exodus (1990)
nodes.detail: Mass displacement of Kashmiri Hindu Pandits from Kashmir Valley, January-March 1990, following killings by militants. ~100,000-300,000 displaced (estimates vary). Governor Jagmohan evacuated many. Became recurring political/communal issue. Government schemes for return continue; limited success.

nodes.label: 65th Amendment Act (1990)
nodes.detail: Added Article 338 — established National Commission for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (combined) with constitutional status. Replaced the earlier office of Special Officer for SCs/STs. Commission bifurcated into NCSC and NCST by 89th Amendment (2003).

nodes.label: 69th Amendment Act (1991) — Delhi NCT
nodes.detail: Inserted Articles 239AA and 239AB giving Delhi 'special status' as National Capital Territory (NCT) with its own legislative assembly and council of ministers. Entries public order, police and land remained with Centre (with LG). Article 239AB allowed President's rule on governor's report. Effective from 1 February 1992.

nodes.label: 71st Amendment Act (1992)
nodes.detail: Added Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali to the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution, bringing total scheduled languages to 18.

nodes.label: 73rd Amendment (1992) — Panchayati Raj
nodes.detail: Inserted Part IX (Articles 243-243O) and 11th Schedule (29 subjects). Granted constitutional status to 3-tier panchayati raj (village, block, district). Mandatory elections every 5 years via State Election Commission; State Finance Commission every 5 years. One-third reservation for women, proportional SC/ST reservation. Effective 24 April 1993 (Panchayati Raj Day).

nodes.label: 74th Amendment (1992) — Municipalities
nodes.detail: Inserted Part IXA (Articles 243P-243ZG) and 12th Schedule (18 subjects). Granted constitutional status to urban local governance — 3 types (Nagar Panchayat, Municipal Council, Municipal Corporation). Mandatory 5-year elections, women reservation, SC/ST reservation, ward committees, district planning committees. Effective 1 June 1993.

nodes.label: 76th Amendment Act (1994) — Tamil Nadu 69% Reservation
nodes.detail: Placed the Tamil Nadu Reservation Act (1993) providing 69% reservation in jobs and educational institutions into the Ninth Schedule, protecting it from judicial review. Intended to exempt Tamil Nadu's reservation policy from the 50% cap set in Indra Sawhney (1992).

nodes.label: 77th Amendment Act (1995) — SC/ST Promotion Reservation
nodes.detail: Added Article 16(4A) — enabled the State to provide reservation in matters of promotion to posts in services in favour of SCs and STs. Countered the Indra Sawhney judgment barring promotion reservation. Further strengthened by 85th, M. Nagaraj and 117th/Jarnail Singh judgments.

nodes.label: 81st Amendment Act (2000) — SC/ST Carry-forward Reservation
nodes.detail: Added Article 16(4B) — allowed the state to treat unfilled SC/ST vacancies as a separate class of vacancies, to be filled in succeeding years, thus breaking the 50% ceiling on reservations as applied to a single year.

nodes.label: 84th Amendment Act (2001) — Delimitation Freeze till 2026
nodes.detail: Extended the freeze on delimitation of Lok Sabha and state assembly constituencies (originally from 42nd Amendment 1976, to 2000) until the first census after 2026. Also allowed readjustment of reserved seats (SC/ST) based on 1991 census. Rationale: to avoid penalising states with effective family planning.

nodes.label: 85th Amendment Act (2001) — Consequential Seniority for SC/ST
nodes.detail: Amended Article 16(4A) to provide 'consequential seniority' to SC/ST candidates promoted through reservation, retrospectively from June 1995. Ensured accelerated seniority — further elaborated by M. Nagaraj (2006) which imposed quantifiable data conditions.

nodes.label: 86th Amendment Act (2002) — Right to Education
nodes.detail: Added Article 21A — 'The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of 6-14 years.' Also added Article 51A(k) duty on parents. Modified Article 45 (early childhood care). Operationalised by RTE Act 2009 (effective 1 April 2010).

nodes.label: 87th Amendment Act (2003) — Delimitation on 2001 Census
nodes.detail: Provided for delimitation of constituencies on the basis of the 2001 census (instead of 1991 census that 84th Amendment permitted). Allowed readjustment of reserved SC/ST seats on 2001 data. 2002 Delimitation Commission (Justice Kuldip Singh) completed work by 2008.

nodes.label: 88th Amendment Act (2003) — Service Tax
nodes.detail: Added Article 268A enabling service tax by Centre, to be collected and appropriated by Centre and states. Inserted Entry 92C (service tax) in Union List. Cleared constitutional basis for service tax regime (introduced 1994 as residual entry). Subsumed under GST by 101st Amendment 2016.

nodes.label: 89th Amendment Act (2003) — NCSC + NCST Separated
nodes.detail: Bifurcated the combined National Commission for SCs and STs (Article 338) into two separate bodies: National Commission for Scheduled Castes (Article 338) and National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (Article 338A). Effective 19 February 2004.

nodes.label: 91st Amendment Act (2003) — Anti-Defection Reform
nodes.detail: Strengthened 10th Schedule (anti-defection): (1) Deleted split exemption (1/3 of party) introduced by 52nd Amendment 1985. (2) Bar on defecting legislators holding ministerial office until re-election or one year. (3) Capped CoM at 15% of Lok Sabha/state assembly strength (min 12). Landmark clean-up of defection politics.

nodes.label: 92nd Amendment Act (2003) — 4 Languages Added
nodes.detail: Added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santhali to the Eighth Schedule, bringing total scheduled languages to 22.

nodes.label: 93rd Amendment Act (2005) — OBC Reservation in Education
nodes.detail: Added Article 15(5) — State can make special provisions for advancement of SEBC, SC, ST including reservation in admissions to private educational institutions except minority institutions. Enabled 27% OBC reservation in central institutions (upheld in Ashoka Thakur 2008).

nodes.label: 95th Amendment Act (2009) — SC/ST/AI Extended to 2020
nodes.detail: Extended SC/ST reservation in Lok Sabha/state assemblies and Anglo-Indian nomination by another 10 years (till 2020). Previously due to expire 2010. Pattern of decadal extensions.

nodes.label: 97th Amendment Act (2011) — Cooperative Societies
nodes.detail: Added Article 43B (DPSP — promote cooperatives) and Part IXB (Articles 243ZH-243ZT) — constitutional status to cooperative societies. 5-year term, democratic elections, women/SC/ST reservation. Right to form cooperative added to Article 19(1)(c). Part IXB partially struck down for multi-state-only application by SC 2021.

nodes.label: 99th Amendment Act (2014) — NJAC (Struck Down)
nodes.detail: Created National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) to replace collegium for judicial appointments to SC/HC. Composition: CJI + 2 senior SC judges + Law Minister + 2 eminent persons. Struck down 16 October 2015 by SC 4-1 in Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Assn v. Union of India case for violating basic structure (judicial independence).

nodes.label: 100th Amendment Act (2015) — India-Bangladesh Land Swap
nodes.detail: Ratified the 1974 Indira-Mujib Agreement (Land Boundary Agreement, LBA). Exchanged 111 Indian enclaves in Bangladesh (17,160 acres) for 51 Bangladeshi enclaves in India (7,110 acres). Amended 1st Schedule. Took effect 1 August 2015. Resolved 6.1 km undemarcated boundary.

nodes.label: 101st Amendment Act (2016) — GST
nodes.detail: Introduced Goods and Services Tax (GST) from 1 July 2017. Added Articles 246A, 269A, 279A (GST Council). Concurrent taxing powers to Centre and States on supply of goods/services. Subsumed VAT, excise, service tax, CST, entertainment tax. Compensation to states for 5 years. Biggest indirect tax reform since independence.

nodes.label: 102nd Amendment Act (2018) — NCBC Constitutional Status
nodes.detail: Conferred constitutional status on the National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC) — established under Article 338B. Also inserted Article 342A for President to specify SEBCs by notification. Impacted state power to identify OBCs (restored by 105th Amendment 2021 after Maratha reservation case).

nodes.label: 103rd Amendment Act (2019) — 10% EWS Reservation
nodes.detail: Added Articles 15(6) and 16(6). Enabled 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) among general category (non-SC/ST/OBC) in jobs and education. Income criteria <Rs 8 lakh annual. Upheld 3-2 by Supreme Court in Janhit Abhiyan (November 2022) despite breaching 50% cap.

nodes.label: 104th Amendment Act (2020)
nodes.detail: Extended SC/ST reservation in Lok Sabha/state assemblies by another 10 years (till 25 January 2030). Removed Anglo-Indian nomination to Lok Sabha and state assemblies. Effective 25 January 2020.

nodes.label: 105th Amendment Act (2021) — State Power to Identify OBCs Restored
nodes.detail: Restored power of states to identify their own Socially and Educationally Backward Classes (SEBCs/OBCs). Overturned effect of 2021 Maratha Reservation case where SC ruled 102nd Amendment had transferred this power exclusively to Centre. Effective 20 September 2021.

nodes.label: 106th Amendment Act (2023) — Nari Shakti Vandan / Women's Reservation
nodes.detail: Women's Reservation Act / Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam. Provided 33% reservation for women in Lok Sabha, state legislative assemblies, and Delhi Assembly. Rotation of reserved seats. Effective after next delimitation (post-2026 census). Ended 27-year-long legislative battle since 1996 draft bill.

nodes.label: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)
nodes.detail: 9-judge SC bench, 11 March 1994. Laid down guidelines for Article 356 (President's Rule): subject to judicial review, floor test required, secularism as basic feature, federalism as basic structure. Dismissed imposition of President's rule on state governments after Babri demolition in some states but upheld Karnataka dismissal. Landmark federalism case.

nodes.label: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997)
nodes.detail: SC (13 August 1997) laid down Vishaka Guidelines for prevention of sexual harassment of women at workplace — using CEDAW as basis. Triggered by gang-rape of Bhanwari Devi, grassroots Rajasthan worker. Guidelines held until Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act 2013.

nodes.label: L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997)
nodes.detail: 7-judge SC bench held Article 323A/323B tribunals cannot exclude jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226/227. Judicial review by High Courts is a basic feature. Tribunals are supplementary, not substitute. Affirmed constitutional framework of judicial review.

nodes.label: M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006)
nodes.detail: 5-judge SC bench upheld 77th, 81st, 82nd, 85th Amendments on reservation in promotion. Imposed 3 conditions: (a) state to demonstrate backwardness, (b) inadequacy of representation, (c) overall administrative efficiency. Partially diluted by Jarnail Singh (2018) — dropped backwardness requirement for SC/ST.

nodes.label: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007)
nodes.detail: 9-judge SC bench, 11 January 2007. Held that laws placed in Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 (Kesavananda) are open to judicial review if they damage basic structure. Also affirmed fundamental rights test including Articles 14, 19, 21. Nullified protection earlier granted by Article 31B.

nodes.label: NJAC Case / SC Advocates-on-Record Assn v. UOI (2015)
nodes.detail: 5-judge SC bench struck down 99th Amendment and NJAC Act (16 October 2015) by 4-1 majority (Khehar, Chelameswar dissenting on merits). Held independence of judiciary is basic feature; NJAC's composition gave executive dominant role in judicial appointments. Revived collegium system.

nodes.label: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (Privacy, 2017)
nodes.detail: 9-judge SC bench, 24 August 2017. Unanimously held Right to Privacy a fundamental right under Articles 14, 19, 21. Overruled M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) to the extent. Triple test — legality, legitimate state aim, proportionality. Basis for Aadhaar verdict 2018, decriminalisation of Section 377, adultery judgments.

nodes.label: Shayara Bano v. UOI (Triple Talaq, 2017)
nodes.detail: 5-judge SC bench, 22 August 2017, struck down triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat) by 3-2 majority as unconstitutional, arbitrary, violative of Article 14. Led to Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act 2019 criminalising triple talaq.

nodes.label: Justice Puttaswamy v. UOI (Aadhaar, 2018)
nodes.detail: 5-judge SC bench, 26 September 2018. Upheld constitutional validity of Aadhaar Act 2016 by 4-1. Limited use to welfare schemes (Section 7); struck down mandatory linkage to bank accounts (Section 57), schools, mobile SIMs. Aadhaar passed as money bill validly. Section 33 (national security disclosure) partially read down.

nodes.label: Navtej Singh Johar v. UOI (Section 377, 2018)
nodes.detail: 5-judge SC bench, 6 September 2018, unanimously decriminalised consensual same-sex relations between adults by partially striking down Section 377 IPC. Overruled Suresh Kumar Koushal (2013). Affirmed LGBTQ+ rights under Articles 14, 15, 19, 21.

nodes.label: Joseph Shine v. UOI (Adultery, 2018)
nodes.detail: 5-judge SC bench, 27 September 2018, unanimously struck down Section 497 IPC (adultery) as unconstitutional. Violated Articles 14, 15, 21. Overruled 1954 Yusuf Abdul Aziz and 1985 Sowmithri Vishnu. Adultery remains civil ground for divorce.

nodes.label: Indian Young Lawyers Assn v. State of Kerala (Sabarimala, 2018)
nodes.detail: 5-judge SC bench, 28 September 2018, by 4-1 struck down ban on entry of women aged 10-50 at Sabarimala temple. Held ban violated Articles 14, 15, 17, 25. Review petitions referred to 9-judge bench (2019); hearing ongoing.

nodes.label: In re Article 370 of the Constitution (2023)
nodes.detail: 5-judge SC bench, 11 December 2023, unanimously upheld abrogation of Article 370 (2019). Held Article 370 was a temporary provision; President's power under Article 370(3) was valid; J&K Reorganisation Act valid. Directed Election Commission to hold J&K assembly elections by September 2024 (held September-October 2024).

nodes.label: Association for Democratic Reforms v. UOI (Electoral Bonds, 2024)
nodes.detail: 5-judge SC bench, 15 February 2024, unanimously struck down Electoral Bonds scheme (2018) as unconstitutional. Held violated Article 19(1)(a) — voter's right to know about political funding. Directed SBI to disclose donor and recipient data. Scheme was based on Finance Act 2017.

nodes.label: National Commission for Women (NCW, 1992)
nodes.detail: Statutory body established under National Commission for Women Act 1990; constituted 31 January 1992. 8 members (Chairperson + 5 members + Member-Secretary). Reviews legal safeguards for women, investigates complaints, advises government. First chairperson: Jayanti Patnaik.

nodes.label: NCBC Statutory (1993)
nodes.detail: National Commission for Backward Classes established under NCBC Act 1993 following Indra Sawhney judgment. Reviewed inclusions/exclusions from OBC list. Made constitutional body via 102nd Amendment (2018) under Article 338B. Advises on OBC list changes via Article 342A.

nodes.label: National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (NCST, 2004)
nodes.detail: Constitutional body under Article 338A (89th Amendment 2003), effective 19 February 2004. Separated from combined NCSC/NCST. 5 members. Protects rights of STs, investigates specific complaints, advises on planning socioeconomic development.

nodes.label: National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR, 2007)
nodes.detail: Statutory body under Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act 2005; constituted March 2007. Ensures all laws/policies consistent with child rights (UNCRC). Chairperson + 6 members. Monitors RTE Act 2009, POCSO Act 2012.

nodes.label: Central Information Commission (CIC, 2005)
nodes.detail: Statutory body under RTI Act 2005. Chief Information Commissioner + up to 10 ICs, appointed by PM-led committee. Hears second appeals on RTI denials. SICs (State) at state level. Term reduced to 3 years by RTI Amendment 2019 (earlier 5 years).

nodes.label: Lokpal (2014)
nodes.detail: Established by Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act 2013, received assent 1 January 2014. Ombudsman to investigate corruption against public servants including PM (limited). Chairperson + 8 members (50% judicial, 50% from SC/ST/OBC/minority/women). First Lokpal Pinaki Chandra Ghose, sworn in 23 March 2019.

nodes.label: Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act 2013
nodes.detail: Passed December 2013 after Anna Hazare movement 2011 and Jan Lokpal campaign. Established Lokpal at Centre, Lokayuktas in states. Covers all public servants including PM (with restrictions on national security etc.). Prior sanction for prosecution of public servants. Amended 2016 (asset declaration).

nodes.label: National Investigation Agency (NIA, 2008)
nodes.detail: Central counter-terrorism agency under NIA Act 2008, established 31 December 2008 post-26/11 Mumbai attacks. Investigates terror-related offences, UAPA cases. Can suo moto take up cases in states. NIA Amendment Act 2019 expanded powers (human trafficking, cyber terror, explosive weapons; extraterritorial jurisdiction).

nodes.label: UIDAI / Aadhaar (2009)
nodes.detail: Unique Identification Authority of India, set up January 2009 under Planning Commission. First Aadhaar issued September 2010. Became statutory body under Aadhaar Act 2016. 12-digit unique biometric+demographic ID. 1.38 billion+ Aadhaars issued by 2024. Upheld with limitations in Puttaswamy Aadhaar 2018.

nodes.label: Aadhaar Act 2016
nodes.detail: Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act 2016. Passed as Money Bill (controversial). Statutory basis for UIDAI. Enabled DBT, PAN linkage. Amendment Act 2019 permitted voluntary use in banking, telecom. Upheld as Money Bill in Puttaswamy-II (2018) but Rojer Mathew case 2019 referred Money Bill question to 7-judge bench.

nodes.label: NITI Aayog (2015)
nodes.detail: National Institution for Transforming India, established 1 January 2015, replaced Planning Commission (1950). Think tank under PM Chair. Governing Council: PM + CMs + LG of UTs. Cooperative and competitive federalism, 3-year action agendas replacing 5-year plans. Aspirational Districts Programme 2018.

nodes.label: NCLT / NCLAT (2016)
nodes.detail: National Company Law Tribunal established 1 June 2016 under Companies Act 2013. Adjudicates company law, IBC insolvency cases, takeovers, oppression/mismanagement. NCLAT appellate body. Replaced Company Law Board, BIFR, AAIFR. 16 benches. Central to IBC 2016 ecosystem.

nodes.label: National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA, 2018)
nodes.detail: Statutory body under Companies Act 2013 (Section 132), operational 1 October 2018. Recommends accounting/auditing standards, monitors compliance, oversees auditors of listed/large public companies. Created post-Satyam/PNB scandals. Reduced ICAI regulatory monopoly.

nodes.label: Chief of Defence Staff (CDS, 2019)
nodes.detail: Four-star military post announced 15 August 2019, operationalised December 2019. Single-point military adviser to government, head of Department of Military Affairs, permanent Chairman COSC. First CDS: Gen Bipin Rawat (Jan 2020-Dec 2021, killed in helicopter crash). Gen Anil Chauhan (Sept 2022-). Theatre commands reform central task.

nodes.label: GST Council (2016)
nodes.detail: Constitutional body under Article 279A (101st Amendment 2016). Chair: Union FM. Members: state FMs. Recommends GST rates, exemptions, thresholds. Decisions need 3/4 majority — centre 1/3 vote, states 2/3. 50+ meetings held. Key body for cooperative federalism on indirect tax.

nodes.label: National Green Tribunal (NGT, 2010)
nodes.detail: Specialised tribunal established under NGT Act 2010, effective 18 October 2010. Adjudicates environmental cases — forests, biodiversity, pollution, environment clearance challenges. Principal Bench New Delhi, 4 zonal benches. Chairperson (former CJ HC+) + judicial + expert members.

nodes.label: Multi-member Election Commission (1993)
nodes.detail: T.N. Seshan appointed CEC in 1990. In October 1993, Narasimha Rao government made EC a 3-member body (CEC + 2 ECs) by ordinance; upheld by SC 1995. Permanent multi-member EC since. Major Seshan-era reforms: voter IDs, code of conduct enforcement, expenditure monitoring. Changed power balance around CEC.

nodes.label: NOTA Introduction (2013)
nodes.detail: 'None of the Above' option on EVMs, introduced September 2013 following PUCL v. Union of India SC judgment (27 Sept 2013). First used in 2013 assembly polls. Provides negative vote option. NOTA votes do not affect winner determination; purely expressive.

nodes.label: VVPAT Introduction (2013)
nodes.detail: Voter-Verifiable Paper Audit Trail, introduced 2013 after Subramanian Swamy v. ECI SC ruling. Piloted in Nagaland Noksen 2013, expanded nationally by 2019 Lok Sabha. Provides paper slip verification of EVM vote. Random VVPAT-EVM matching — 5 per assembly segment (post-Chandrachud 2024 hearing).

nodes.label: Electoral Bonds Scheme (2017-2024)
nodes.detail: Introduced Finance Act 2017 (Money Bill), notified 2 January 2018. Banking instrument for anonymous corporate donations to political parties. SBI issued bonds in Rs 1k-1cr denominations. Total Rs 16,518 crore issued by 2024. Struck down as unconstitutional by SC on 15 February 2024 (ADR v. UOI).

nodes.label: CEC and Election Commissioners Act 2023
nodes.detail: Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act 2023. Replaced SC's 2023 Anoop Baranwal interim mechanism (PM-LOP-CJI). New selection committee: PM, LoP (or largest opposition leader), Union Minister (nominated by PM). Status equivalent to Cabinet Secretary (not SC judge).

nodes.label: Three New Criminal Laws (2023) — BNS, BNSS, BSA
nodes.detail: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) replaced IPC 1860; Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) replaced CrPC 1973; Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) replaced Indian Evidence Act 1872. Passed December 2023, effective 1 July 2024. New offences (mob lynching, terrorism, organised crime). Removed Section 124A sedition, replaced by stricter Section 152.

nodes.label: Article 370 Abrogation (5 August 2019)
nodes.detail: President's order CO 272 (5 Aug) and CO 273 (6 Aug) revoked special status of J&K under Article 370. J&K Reorganisation Act 2019 bifurcated state into UTs of J&K (with legislature) and Ladakh (without). Net result: Article 370 rendered inoperative, all central laws extended. Upheld by SC 5-judge bench December 2023.

nodes.label: Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) 2019
nodes.detail: Enacted 11 December 2019. Expedited Indian citizenship for Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis, Christians from Afghanistan/Bangladesh/Pakistan who entered before 31 December 2014. Excluded Muslims. Triggered nationwide protests (Shaheen Bagh Dec 2019-Mar 2020). Rules notified March 2024. Constitutional validity sub judice.

nodes.label: Anna Hazare / India Against Corruption (2011)
nodes.detail: Nationwide anti-corruption movement 2011-12 led by Anna Hazare, Arvind Kejriwal, Kiran Bedi, Prashant Bhushan. Hunger strikes at Jantar Mantar (April 2011) and Ramlila Maidan (Aug 2011). Demanded Jan Lokpal Bill. Led to Lokpal Act 2013, birth of Aam Aadmi Party 2012, UPA-II legitimacy crisis.

nodes.label: Nirbhaya Case (December 2012)
nodes.detail: Brutal gang rape and murder of physiotherapy intern 'Nirbhaya' in Delhi, 16 December 2012. Triggered nationwide protests and legal reform. Justice Verma Committee (Jan 2013). Criminal Law (Amendment) Act 2013 — new offences (acid attack, voyeurism, stalking), harsher rape penalties. Four convicts hanged 20 March 2020.

nodes.label: Farm Laws 2020 → Repeal 2021
nodes.detail: Three farm laws enacted September 2020: Farmers' Produce Trade and Commerce Act; Farmers (Empowerment and Protection) Agreement on Price Assurance Act; Essential Commodities (Amendment) Act. Triggered year-long Delhi border farmer protests. Repealed via Farm Laws Repeal Act November 2021. Key issue: MSP statutory guarantee.

nodes.label: Private Bank Licences (1993)
nodes.detail: RBI granted new bank licences to private sector in 1993-94 based on Narasimham I — first since 1969 nationalisation. First round: HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, UTI Bank (Axis), IndusInd, Centurion, Global Trust, Bank of Punjab, Times Bank, Development Credit, IDBI Bank. Second round 2003-04, third 2013-14 (Bandhan, IDFC).

nodes.label: Monetary Policy Committee (MPC, 2016)
nodes.detail: 6-member committee under RBI Act (amended 2016). 3 RBI (Governor chair, Deputy Governor, executive director) + 3 government nominees. Sets policy repo rate by majority. First meeting October 2016. Targets CPI inflation 4±2% (flexible inflation targeting). Replaced Governor-only monetary policy decisions.

nodes.label: Flexible Inflation Targeting (2016)
nodes.detail: Formal inflation targeting framework agreed in Monetary Policy Framework Agreement (20 Feb 2015) between RBI and Government; enshrined in RBI Act amendment 2016. Target: CPI headline inflation 4±2% over 5-year period. Reset every 5 years (renewed 2021). Replaced multiple-indicator approach.

nodes.label: PSB Mega-Mergers (2017-2020)
nodes.detail: Consolidation of public sector banks: 5 SBI associates + BMB merged into SBI 1 April 2017 (SBI became top-50 global). Vijaya+Dena+Bank of Baroda merged 1 April 2019. 10 more banks merged into 4 w.e.f. 1 April 2020: OBC+UBI+PNB; Syndicate+Canara; Andhra+Corp+Union; Allahabad+Indian. Reduced PSBs from 27 (2017) to 12 (2020).

nodes.label: Asset Quality Review (AQR, 2015)
nodes.detail: RBI Governor Raghuram Rajan-driven Asset Quality Review of PSB loan books, July 2015. Forced banks to reclassify stressed loans as NPAs, doubling NPA levels to 11.5% of gross advances by 2018. Catalysed IBC 2016, PSB recapitalisation, bank mergers. Triggered Rajan-Government friction.

nodes.label: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) 2016
nodes.detail: Consolidated insolvency laws for companies and individuals. Passed May 2016. Time-bound 180-day (extendable to 270 days, later 330 days) Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) through NCLT. IBBI as regulator. Creditor-in-control regime. Essar Steel, Bhushan Steel, Jet Airways major cases. Credited with ~30%+ recovery of stressed assets.

nodes.label: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI, 2016)
nodes.detail: Statutory body under IBC 2016, established 1 October 2016. Regulator for insolvency professionals, insolvency professional agencies, information utilities. Framed CIRP, liquidation, voluntary liquidation regulations. Works with NCLT/NCLAT as adjudicator.

nodes.label: Demonetisation (8 November 2016)
nodes.detail: Withdrawal of Rs 500 and Rs 1000 notes (86% of currency by value) by PM Modi's 8 November 2016 announcement. Replaced by new Rs 500 and Rs 2000. Goals: curb black money, counterfeit currency, terror financing, push digital. 99.3% of demonetised notes returned to banks. Upheld 4-1 by SC January 2023. Rs 2000 note withdrawn 2023.

nodes.label: GST Launch (1 July 2017)
nodes.detail: Goods and Services Tax went live 1 July 2017 (midnight Parliament session). Multi-slab: 0, 5, 12, 18, 28% + cess on demerit/luxury. CGST + SGST + IGST structure. Subsumed VAT, central excise, service tax, CST, entry tax, entertainment tax. GSTN IT backbone. E-way bill, e-invoice progressive rollout. Revenue neutral rate hit gradually.

nodes.label: GSTN (Goods and Services Tax Network)
nodes.detail: IT backbone for GST, set up as Section 8 (non-profit) company in March 2013; converted to government-owned entity 2018 (51% Centre + states). Handles return filing, payment, e-way bills, registration for 1.4 crore+ taxpayers. Managed by Infosys contractually.

nodes.label: Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY, 2014)
nodes.detail: Financial inclusion scheme launched 28 August 2014. Zero-balance savings accounts, RuPay debit card, Rs 1 lakh accident insurance, Rs 30k life insurance, overdraft facility. Opened 52 crore+ accounts by 2024, over Rs 2.3 lakh crore deposits. Backbone of DBT and JAM trinity.

nodes.label: JAM Trinity (Jan Dhan + Aadhaar + Mobile)
nodes.detail: Policy framework linking Jan Dhan accounts + Aadhaar + Mobile numbers for direct benefit transfer and financial inclusion. Popularised by Economic Survey 2014-15 (Arvind Subramanian). Enabled DBT of LPG subsidy (PAHAL), MGNREGA wages, pensions, scholarships — reducing leakages. ~Rs 34 lakh crore DBT transferred by 2024.

nodes.label: Swachh Bharat Mission (2014)
nodes.detail: Sanitation mission launched 2 October 2014 (Gandhi Jayanti). SBM-Gramin (Ministry Jal Shakti) + SBM-Urban (Ministry Housing/Urban Affairs). Built 11+ crore individual household latrines; India declared ODF October 2019 (Gandhi's 150th birth anniversary). SBM 2.0 launched 2021 focus on ODF-Plus, waste management.

nodes.label: Make in India (2014)
nodes.detail: Initiative launched 25 September 2014 to promote manufacturing and increase sector share in GDP from 16% to 25% by 2022 (target later revised). 25 focus sectors. Ease of doing business push (India rose from 142 in 2014 to 63 in 2020 World Bank EoDB). Make in India 2.0 with PLI schemes from 2020.

nodes.label: PM MUDRA Yojana (2015)
nodes.detail: Micro Units Development and Refinance Agency Ltd. Launched 8 April 2015. Loans to non-corporate, non-farm small/micro enterprises up to Rs 10 lakh (raised to Rs 20 lakh in 2024). Three categories: Shishu (<Rs 50k), Kishore (Rs 50k-5L), Tarun (Rs 5-10L). Tarun Plus up to Rs 20L (2024). Collateral-free. 45+ crore loans sanctioned.

nodes.label: PM Ujjwala Yojana (2016)
nodes.detail: Launched 1 May 2016. Free LPG connections to women from BPL households (target 5 crore by 2019, extended to 8 crore). Ujjwala 2.0 (2021) added migrants. 10+ crore connections released by 2024. Addressed biomass cooking smoke health/gender issue.

nodes.label: Ayushman Bharat / PM-JAY (2018)
nodes.detail: World's largest health assurance scheme launched 23 September 2018. PM Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY) — Rs 5 lakh annual health cover per family to 12 crore poor/vulnerable families. Health and Wellness Centres (HWCs) arm. 6+ crore hospital admissions by 2024. Implementation via National Health Authority (NHA).

nodes.label: Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Schemes (2020)
nodes.detail: Manufacturing incentive scheme launched March 2020 (mobile phones) initial. Expanded to 14 sectors 2021 — electronics, pharma, automobiles, advanced chemistry cell batteries, textiles, specialty steel, food processing, white goods etc. Rs 1.97 lakh crore outlay over 5 years. Incentives 4-6% of incremental sales linked to output targets.

nodes.label: Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan (2020)
nodes.detail: Self-reliant India campaign announced 12 May 2020 by PM Modi amid COVID-19 lockdown. Rs 20 lakh crore stimulus (10% of GDP) — fiscal + monetary + RBI measures. Five pillars: Economy, Infrastructure, System, Demography, Demand. Included MSME ECLGS, agri reforms, PLI, privatisation push, Minimum Govt.

nodes.label: COVID-19 Lockdown (25 March 2020)
nodes.detail: Nationwide lockdown from 25 March 2020 (initial 21 days, extended in phases till 31 May 2020). One of the strictest globally. GDP contracted 6.6% in FY2020-21 (first contraction since 1979). Migrant labour crisis April-May. PMGKAY food grain scheme announced 26 March 2020. Vaccine rollout 16 January 2021.

nodes.label: COVID-19 Vaccination (January 2021)
nodes.detail: World's largest vaccination drive launched 16 January 2021. Two domestic vaccines — Covaxin (Bharat Biotech, indigenous) and Covishield (SII, AstraZeneca licensed). Free universal vaccination from 21 June 2021. 220+ crore doses administered by 2023. Co-WIN platform for registration/certificate.

nodes.label: PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana (PMGKAY, 2020)
nodes.detail: Free food grain scheme launched 26 March 2020 amid COVID lockdown. 5 kg wheat/rice per person per month free (over and above NFSA PDS). 80 crore beneficiaries. Multiple extensions. Integrated with NFSA from 1 January 2023. Cumulative Rs 3.9 lakh crore + by 2023.

nodes.label: Unified Payments Interface (UPI, 2016)
nodes.detail: Real-time mobile payment system developed by NPCI, launched 11 April 2016. Instant inter-bank transfers via VPA (Virtual Payment Address), QR code. Transformed India's payments landscape. Crossed 14 billion monthly transactions (2024), Rs 20+ lakh crore monthly value. Major players: PhonePe, Google Pay, Paytm. UPI Lite, UPI on credit card extensions.

nodes.label: National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI, 2008)
nodes.detail: Umbrella organisation for retail payments in India, established December 2008 under Payment and Settlement Systems Act 2007. Not-for-profit (Section 8). Products: NFS (ATM), IMPS, RuPay (2012), AePS, APBS, NACH, UPI (2016), BHIM. Shareholders: 56 banks. RBI regulator.

nodes.label: Digital India Programme (2015)
nodes.detail: Launched 1 July 2015. Nine pillars: broadband highways, mobile connectivity, public internet access, e-governance, eKranti, information for all, electronics manufacturing, IT for jobs, early harvest programmes. Flagship projects: BharatNet, DigiLocker, MyGov, e-Hospital, CSCs. Partner to JAM, UPI.

nodes.label: 5G Rollout in India (October 2022)
nodes.detail: 5G services launched 1 October 2022 by PM Modi at India Mobile Congress. Reliance Jio (standalone), Airtel (NSA) led rollout. Fastest global 5G rollout — 4+ lakh base stations covering all districts by 2024. Spectrum auctions 2022 (Rs 1.5 lakh crore). Manufacturing boost via PLI for telecom.

nodes.label: 2008 Global Financial Crisis
nodes.detail: Subprime mortgage crisis in US triggered Lehman Brothers collapse (15 September 2008), cascading global liquidity freeze, recession. India's GDP growth fell from 9.3% (2007-08) to 6.7% (2008-09) but rebounded quickly due to domestic demand, banking sector insulation, stimulus. RBI cut rates, fiscal packages Dec 2008, Jan/Feb 2009.

nodes.label: National Food Security Act 2013
nodes.detail: Enacted 10 September 2013. Legal entitlement to subsidised food grains to 75% rural, 50% urban population (~67% of total). 5 kg/person/month at Rs 1/2/3 per kg (coarse grains/wheat/rice). Antyodaya households 35 kg per family. Pregnant/lactating women and children nutrition support via ICDS and mid-day meal.

nodes.label: Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013 (RFCTLARR)
nodes.detail: Enacted 27 September 2013, replaced colonial Land Acquisition Act 1894. Four-times compensation for rural land, two-times for urban. Consent requirement: 70% private, 80% PPP. Social Impact Assessment. R&R package, food security impact check. NDA attempted amendment 2015 — rolled back on protests.

nodes.label: Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT, 2013)
nodes.detail: Launched 1 January 2013 by UPA-II. Direct transfer of subsidies and benefits to Aadhaar-linked/bank-linked beneficiary accounts, cutting leakages. Started with scholarships, LPG. Expanded to 310+ schemes. Rs 34 lakh crore+ transferred by 2023. Enabled by JAM trinity.

nodes.label: Inflation Targeting Framework Agreement (February 2015)
nodes.detail: Monetary Policy Framework Agreement between Government of India and RBI signed 20 February 2015. Formalised flexible inflation targeting (CPI 4±2%). Basis for RBI Act amendment 2016 and MPC. Urjit Patel Committee recommendation.

nodes.label: Fiscal Stimulus 2008-09
nodes.detail: Three stimulus packages in response to global crisis — 7 December 2008, 2 January 2009, 24 February 2009. CENVAT and service tax cuts, plan expenditure boost, export incentives. Fiscal deficit rose from 2.5% (2007-08) to 6% (2008-09). Triggered expansionary trend that worsened into 2013 taper tantrum.

nodes.label: Taper Tantrum (2013)
nodes.detail: May 2013 Bernanke hint of Fed tapering QE triggered capital outflows from emerging markets. Rupee fell 20%+ (Rs 55 to Rs 68 per USD, Aug 2013). RBI emergency measures — USD swap window, rate hike, gold import curbs. Raghuram Rajan took charge as RBI Governor 4 September 2013.

nodes.label: Raghuram Rajan (RBI Governor 2013-16)
nodes.detail: 23rd RBI Governor, 4 September 2013 to 4 September 2016. Stabilised rupee post-taper tantrum. Architect of monetary policy framework reforms, inflation targeting, AQR 2015. Controversial exit amidst political friction. Later at University of Chicago.

nodes.label: Urjit Patel (RBI Governor 2016-18)
nodes.detail: 24th RBI Governor, 5 September 2016 to 10 December 2018. Chaired Patel Committee whose recommendations underpinned inflation targeting. Demonetisation happened in early tenure. Resigned amid government-RBI friction over surplus transfer, PCA norms, payment regulator autonomy.

nodes.label: Urjit Patel Committee (2014)
nodes.detail: RBI's Expert Committee to Revise and Strengthen Monetary Policy Framework, chaired by Deputy Governor Urjit Patel, reported January 2014. Recommended CPI as nominal anchor (replacing WPI), inflation target 4%, MPC structure. Basis for 2015 MPF Agreement and 2016 RBI Act amendment.

nodes.label: Chelliah Tax Reform Committee (1991-92)
nodes.detail: Chaired by economist Raja Chelliah. Reports 1992-93. Recommended comprehensive tax reform — moderate rates, broad base, phasing out exemptions, VAT, simplified customs. Foundation for 1990s-2000s tax reforms including income tax rate cuts, service tax 1994, corporate tax cuts.

nodes.label: Raja J. Chelliah (Architect of Tax Reforms)
nodes.detail: Indian public finance economist (1922-2009), 'Father of Indian Tax Reforms'. Chaired Tax Reform Committee 1991-92. Earlier with IMF (1960-69), NIPFP founder-director (1976-92). Padma Vibhushan 2007. Influenced post-1991 tax architecture.

nodes.label: Planning Commission Abolished (2014)
nodes.detail: PM Modi announced abolition of Planning Commission in Independence Day speech, 15 August 2014. Replaced by NITI Aayog from 1 January 2015. Criticised for top-down approach, inflexibility. Final Twelfth Plan (2012-17) ran its course; no 13th Plan.

nodes.label: UDAY Scheme (2015)
nodes.detail: Ujwal DISCOM Assurance Yojana, launched November 2015. Financial turnaround of state electricity distribution companies. States took over 75% DISCOM debt (Rs 2 lakh crore), issued bonds. Aimed at operational efficiency and aggregate technical & commercial losses reduction. Mixed results; many states fell back.

nodes.label: Sovereign Gold Bonds (2015)
nodes.detail: Scheme launched 5 November 2015 to reduce gold imports demand. Tradable bonds issued by RBI on behalf of Government, denominated in grams of gold. 8-year tenor, 2.5% fixed interest. Capital gains tax exempt on redemption. Rs 72,000+ crore mobilised by 2024.

nodes.label: Ease of Doing Business Rise (2014-20)
nodes.detail: India moved from 142nd (2014) to 63rd (2020) in World Bank Ease of Doing Business Index — 79-spot jump. Major reforms: single-window registration, faster construction permits, contract enforcement, insolvency (IBC 2016), tax simplification. World Bank discontinued EoDB from 2021 after methodology issues.

nodes.label: PM Gati Shakti National Master Plan (2021)
nodes.detail: Launched 13 October 2021. Multi-modal connectivity infrastructure master plan. Integrates 16 ministries (Roads, Railways, Shipping, Telecom, Power, Petroleum, Aviation etc.) onto single GIS digital platform. National Logistics Policy (17 Sept 2022) complements. Target: reduce logistics cost from 13-14% to 8% of GDP.

nodes.label: India's G20 Presidency (Dec 2022 - Nov 2023)
nodes.detail: India held G20 Presidency 1 December 2022 to 30 November 2023. Theme: 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' / 'One Earth, One Family, One Future'. Delhi Declaration (9 Sept 2023) unanimous. African Union admitted as G20 member. Global Biofuel Alliance, India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) launched. Digital Public Infrastructure highlight.

nodes.label: Earth Summit / UNCED Rio (1992)
nodes.detail: UN Conference on Environment and Development, Rio de Janeiro, 3-14 June 1992. 172 nations participated. Produced Rio Declaration, Agenda 21, Statement on Forest Principles. Opened for signature: UNFCCC and CBD. Marked mainstreaming of sustainable development. India a prominent voice for CBDR principle.

nodes.label: Agenda 21 (1992)
nodes.detail: Non-binding action plan on sustainable development adopted at Earth Summit 1992, Rio. 40 chapters, 4 sections — social/economic dimensions, conservation, strengthening major groups' role, means of implementation. UN Commission on Sustainable Development (CSD) created to follow through (dissolved 2013, replaced by HLPF).

nodes.label: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC, 1992)
nodes.detail: Opened for signature at Rio Earth Summit 1992; entered into force 21 March 1994. Framework treaty with 198 parties (2024). Objective: stabilise GHG concentrations at levels preventing dangerous anthropogenic interference. CBDR (Common But Differentiated Responsibilities) principle. Annual COP. Secretariat in Bonn.

nodes.label: Kyoto Protocol (1997)
nodes.detail: UNFCCC Protocol adopted 11 December 1997 at COP3 Kyoto; entered force 16 February 2005. Binding GHG reduction targets for Annex I (developed) countries — avg 5.2% below 1990 by 2008-12 (first commitment period). Flexibility mechanisms: CDM, JI, ET. Second commitment period 2013-20 (Doha Amendment). US never ratified.

nodes.label: COP15 Copenhagen (2009)
nodes.detail: 15th Conference of Parties to UNFCCC, December 2009. 'Copenhagen Accord' — non-binding political declaration. Kept 2°C target; $100bn/year climate finance pledge by developed nations by 2020. India's PM Manmohan Singh intervention with China, Brazil, South Africa (BASIC group) shaped outcome. India first pledged voluntary 20-25% emissions intensity reduction.

nodes.label: Paris Agreement (2015)
nodes.detail: Adopted at COP21 Paris, 12 December 2015; entered force 4 November 2016. Goal: limit global warming to well below 2°C, pursuing 1.5°C above pre-industrial. Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs). 5-year review cycle (global stocktake). $100bn climate finance target; Loss and Damage dialogue. US withdrew 2020, rejoined 2021.

nodes.label: India's INDC (2015)
nodes.detail: Intended Nationally Determined Contribution submitted to UNFCCC on 2 October 2015. Three quantitative targets by 2030: (1) reduce emissions intensity of GDP by 33-35% from 2005 levels, (2) 40% cumulative electric power from non-fossil sources, (3) additional carbon sink of 2.5-3 billion tonnes CO2 via forests. Updated NDC 2022 with more ambitious targets.

nodes.label: COP26 Glasgow (2021) — India's Panchamrit
nodes.detail: UN Climate Conference in Glasgow, 1-12 November 2021. PM Modi announced India's Panchamrit (five nectar elements): Non-fossil capacity 500 GW by 2030; 50% energy from renewables; reduce emissions by 1bn tonnes; emissions intensity cut 45% (up from 33-35%); Net Zero by 2070. Glasgow Climate Pact — phase-down coal (not phase-out).

nodes.label: India's Updated NDC (August 2022)
nodes.detail: India submitted updated Nationally Determined Contribution to UNFCCC 26 August 2022. Quantified two Panchamrit elements: 45% emissions intensity cut by 2030 from 2005 (up from 33-35%); 50% cumulative installed capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030 (up from 40%). Mission LiFE — Lifestyle for Environment added as theme.

nodes.label: COP28 Dubai (2023) — Loss & Damage Fund
nodes.detail: UN Climate Conference in Dubai/UAE, 30 November - 13 December 2023. First Global Stocktake. Loss and Damage Fund operationalised (first agreed at COP27 Sharm el-Sheikh 2022). UAE Consensus called for 'transitioning away from fossil fuels'. 118 countries pledged to triple renewables by 2030. Agriculture inclusion, health day introduced.

nodes.label: Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD, 1992)
nodes.detail: International treaty opened for signature at Rio 1992, entered force 29 December 1993. Three objectives: biodiversity conservation, sustainable use of components, fair and equitable benefit-sharing from genetic resources. Two protocols: Cartagena (2000, biosafety), Nagoya (2010, ABS). 196 parties (US signed but not ratified).

nodes.label: Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (2000)
nodes.detail: Protocol to CBD, adopted 29 January 2000 Montreal; entered force 11 September 2003. Governs transboundary movement, handling, use of living modified organisms (LMOs/GMOs). Advance Informed Agreement procedure. India party since 17 January 2003.

nodes.label: Nagoya Protocol on ABS (2010)
nodes.detail: Protocol to CBD on Access and Benefit-Sharing (ABS), adopted at COP10 Nagoya 29 October 2010; entered force 12 October 2014. Fair/equitable sharing of benefits arising from genetic resource use and associated traditional knowledge. India party since 9 October 2012.

nodes.label: Stockholm Convention on POPs (2001)
nodes.detail: Treaty on Persistent Organic Pollutants adopted 22 May 2001; entered force 17 May 2004. Eliminates/restricts 12 initial POPs (dirty dozen) — PCBs, DDT, dioxins, furans etc. List expanded over COPs. India ratified 13 January 2006.

nodes.label: Minamata Convention on Mercury (2013)
nodes.detail: Global treaty adopted 10 October 2013 Kumamoto, Japan; entered force 16 August 2017. Protects human health and environment from anthropogenic mercury. Named after Minamata disease from mercury poisoning in Japan. India party since 18 June 2018.

nodes.label: Kigali Amendment to Montreal Protocol (2016)
nodes.detail: Amendment to Montreal Protocol (1987, on ozone) adopted 15 October 2016 Kigali, Rwanda; entered force 1 January 2019. Phases down HFCs — powerful GHGs used as ODS substitutes. Can avoid 0.4°C warming by 2100. India ratified 27 September 2021, committed to 80% phase-down by 2047.

nodes.label: Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs, 2015)
nodes.detail: UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development adopted 25 September 2015 New York. 17 Goals, 169 targets, ~230 indicators. Replaced Millennium Development Goals (2000-15). Universal applicability (developed + developing). NITI Aayog nodal body for India; SDG India Index published annually.

nodes.label: Millennium Development Goals (MDGs, 2000)
nodes.detail: UN Millennium Declaration adopted 8 September 2000. 8 goals, 21 targets, 60 indicators for period 2000-15. Focused on poverty, education, gender, child/maternal mortality, HIV, environment, global partnership. Succeeded by SDGs in 2015.

nodes.label: Biological Diversity Act 2002
nodes.detail: Enacted 5 February 2003 to implement CBD 1992. Three-tier structure: NBA (Chennai), SBBs (state level), BMCs (local, 2.7 lakh+). Regulates access to biological resources, benefit-sharing. Amendment Act 2023 — simplified AYUSH/traditional practitioner processes. Criminal offences decriminalised to civil.

nodes.label: National Biodiversity Authority (NBA, 2003)
nodes.detail: Statutory body under Biological Diversity Act 2002, established October 2003 at Chennai. Regulates access to India's biological resources and traditional knowledge by foreign entities. Advises government on conservation measures. Divya Pharmacy case (Uttarakhand HC 2018) extended scope to domestic entities.

nodes.label: National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC, 2008)
nodes.detail: India's domestic climate strategy announced 30 June 2008 by PM Manmohan Singh. 8 National Missions: Solar, Enhanced Energy Efficiency, Sustainable Habitat, Water, Sustaining Himalayan Ecosystem, Green India, Sustainable Agriculture, Strategic Knowledge. State Action Plans (SAPCCs) followed. Expanded post-2015 with Mission LiFE, Wind, Health, Coastal.

nodes.label: Jawaharlal Nehru National Solar Mission (JNNSM, 2010)
nodes.detail: One of 8 NAPCC missions launched 11 January 2010. Target initially 20 GW solar by 2022; revised to 100 GW (2015), 280 GW by 2030 in updated NDC. Component: grid-connected, off-grid, solar manufacturing. Implemented via MNRE + SECI. India solar capacity 85+ GW by 2024.

nodes.label: Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act (CAMPA, 2016)
nodes.detail: Enacted 3 August 2016, operationalised August 2018. Statutory framework for CAMPA — Rs 66,000+ crore corpus from forest diversion levies. National CAMPA at Centre, State CAMPA. Spends on afforestation, catchment protection, wildlife management. Replaces ad-hoc CAMPA regime since 2004 Godavarman case direction.

nodes.label: Namami Gange Programme (2014)
nodes.detail: Integrated Ganga Conservation Mission, approved June 2014 with Rs 20,000 crore initial outlay. Implemented by National Mission for Clean Ganga (NMCG). Components: sewerage infrastructure, river-front, surface cleaning, afforestation, biodiversity. Extended to 2026 with Rs 42,500+ crore. 'Gangatatva' included Ghat development.

nodes.label: Ganga Declared National River (2008)
nodes.detail: Ganga accorded status of India's National River on 4 November 2008 by PM Manmohan Singh. Creation of National Ganga River Basin Authority (NGRBA) February 2009 under Environment Protection Act 1986 with PM as chair. Framework for basin-level conservation — precursor to NMCG (2011) and Namami Gange (2014).

nodes.label: International Solar Alliance (ISA, 2015)
nodes.detail: India-France joint initiative launched at COP21 Paris, 30 November 2015. 121 solar-rich countries between Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn eligible; expanded to all UN members 2020. Framework Agreement entered force 6 December 2017. Treaty-based intergovernmental org, HQ at NISE Gurugram. Focus: deploy 1000 GW solar by 2030, mobilise $1 trillion.

nodes.label: Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI, 2019)
nodes.detail: India-led international partnership launched at UN Climate Summit 23 September 2019 by PM Modi. Promotes climate- and disaster-resilient infrastructure. 40+ member countries and institutions. HQ at New Delhi. Programmes: IRIS (Infrastructure for Resilient Island States), DRI CoE.

nodes.label: IPCC Assessment Reports (AR4 2007, AR5 2014, AR6 2021-23)
nodes.detail: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change reports: AR4 (2007, 4°C warming risk; Nobel Peace Prize); AR5 (2013-14, 95% anthropogenic attribution certainty); AR6 (2021-23 in three Working Group reports + synthesis March 2023 — 'Code Red for Humanity'). Scientific basis for UNFCCC/Paris Agreement targets.

nodes.label: Perform Achieve Trade (PAT, 2012)
nodes.detail: Market-based energy efficiency scheme under National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency (NMEEE/NAPCC). PAT Cycle I (2012-15). Covers designated consumers in 13 sectors. Energy Saving Certificates (ESCerts) tradable on IEX. Saved ~1.5% of national electricity consumption. Part of emerging domestic carbon market.

nodes.label: Indian Carbon Market (2023)
nodes.detail: Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act 2022 enabled Carbon Credit Trading Scheme. CCTS notified 28 June 2023. Regulator: BEE (Bureau of Energy Efficiency). Compliance mechanism for hard-to-abate sectors (industry, power) + voluntary market for offsets. First issuance expected 2025-26.

nodes.label: National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023)
nodes.detail: Approved by Union Cabinet 4 January 2023. Rs 19,744 crore outlay. Target: 5 MMT annual green hydrogen production by 2030; 60-100 GW electrolyser capacity; reduce 50 MMT CO2 emissions; cut $100bn import bill. Components: SIGHT (incentives), Green Hydrogen Hubs, R&D, skill development.

nodes.label: Mission LiFE / Lifestyle for Environment (2022)
nodes.detail: Launched by PM Modi at COP26 Glasgow (Nov 2021); formally launched with UN Secretary-General 20 October 2022 at Kevadia. Focus on behaviour change towards environmentally conscious lifestyles. 'Pro-Planet People' framework. Integrated into India's updated NDC 2022 as theme.

nodes.label: Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) Notification 2019
nodes.detail: CRZ 2019 notified 18 January 2019 under Environment Protection Act 1986, replacing CRZ 2011. 4 zones: CRZ-I (ecologically sensitive), CRZ-II (developed municipal), CRZ-III (relatively undisturbed rural), CRZ-IV (water body). Relaxations for tourism infrastructure, floor space index, land-use near HTL. Implemented by state coastal zone authorities.

nodes.label: Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules 2017
nodes.detail: Notified 26 September 2017 under Environment Protection Act 1986, replacing 2010 rules. Decentralised governance — empowered State Wetland Authorities. List of prohibited activities. Basis for identifying/protecting India's ~200 Ramsar sites (target). India had 80+ Ramsar sites by 2024, highest in Asia.

nodes.label: Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016 (+2022 EPR)
nodes.detail: Notified 18 March 2016 under EPA. Extended to all urban areas + rural areas near urban. Key provisions: minimum thickness 50 microns (later 75, 120 microns), multilayered plastic phase-out, EPR. 2021 Amendment banned single-use plastic items from 1 July 2022. 2022 Amendment introduced formal EPR (Extended Producer Responsibility) registration.

nodes.label: E-Waste Management Rules 2022
nodes.detail: Notified 2 November 2022, effective 1 April 2023, replacing 2016 rules. Introduced mandatory EPR registration on online portal; EPR certificates tradable; included new items (solar PV modules, toys with electronics). Producers, manufacturers, refurbishers covered. CPCB as nodal authority.

nodes.label: India's Ramsar Sites Growth (26 → 80+ sites)
nodes.detail: India acceded to Ramsar Convention 1 February 1982. Only 26 sites till 2020, then rapid designation: 2022 saw 28 new sites in one year (unprecedented). Total 85 Ramsar sites by July 2024 (highest in Asia; 3rd globally after UK, Mexico). Total wetland area covered ~13.3 lakh hectares.

nodes.label: Kutiyattam (UNESCO ICH, 2008)
nodes.detail: Sanskrit theatre of Kerala, performed by Chakyar community. Recognised by UNESCO as Masterpiece of Oral and Intangible Heritage 2001; inscribed on Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008. One of India's oldest living theatrical traditions (2000+ years). Uses Mizhavu percussion.

nodes.label: Ramlila (UNESCO ICH, 2008)
nodes.detail: Traditional folk theatre of North India re-enacting the Ramayana. Inscribed UNESCO ICH Representative List 2008. Best-known productions at Ramnagar (Varanasi), Ayodhya, Ramleela Maidan Delhi. Staged during Sharad Navaratras leading up to Dussehra. Multiple regional variations.

nodes.label: Vedic Chanting (UNESCO ICH, 2008)
nodes.detail: Oral tradition of chanting Vedic mantras, among oldest continuous oral traditions. UNESCO Masterpiece of Oral and Intangible Heritage 2003; Representative List 2008. Multiple pathas (recitation styles). Community: Vedic Brahmin families across India.

nodes.label: Ramman (UNESCO ICH, 2009)
nodes.detail: Religious ritual and theatre festival of Saloor-Dungra village, Chamoli district, Uttarakhand. Hosted by Bhumiyal Devta deity, performed with masks and jagars. UNESCO ICH Representative List inscription 2009.

nodes.label: Mudiyettu (UNESCO ICH, 2010)
nodes.detail: Ritual theatre and dance drama of Kerala depicting battle of Goddess Kali and demon Darika. Performed in Bhagavati Kavu temples Feb-May. UNESCO ICH Representative List 2010.

nodes.label: Kalbelia (UNESCO ICH, 2010)
nodes.detail: Folk dance and songs of Kalbelia nomadic tribe of Rajasthan, traditionally snake-catchers. Women perform in black swirling skirts mimicking serpent movements. UNESCO ICH Representative List 2010.

nodes.label: Chhau (UNESCO ICH, 2010)
nodes.detail: Tribal martial dance of eastern India — Purulia (West Bengal), Seraikella (Jharkhand), Mayurbhanj (Odisha) styles. UNESCO ICH Representative List 2010. Mayurbhanj Chhau uses no masks. Recognised as 9th classical dance form by Sangeet Natak Akademi.

nodes.label: Buddhist Chanting of Ladakh (UNESCO ICH, 2012)
nodes.detail: Recitation of sacred Buddhist texts in trans-Himalayan Ladakh region. UNESCO ICH Representative List 2012. Includes Palyul, Nyingma, Drikung, Sakya, Gelug lineage chanting. Performed by monks and nuns in monasteries.

nodes.label: Sankirtana (UNESCO ICH, 2013)
nodes.detail: Ritual singing, drumming and dancing of Manipuri Vaishnavas, narrating life of Krishna. UNESCO ICH Representative List 2013. 2 drummers + 10 singer-dancers in courtyard halls. Reinforces devotional community bonds.

nodes.label: Thatheras of Jandiala Guru (UNESCO ICH, 2014)
nodes.detail: Traditional brass and copper utensil-making craft of Thathera community in Jandiala Guru, Punjab. UNESCO ICH Representative List 2014. Metals: brass, copper, kansa. Produced utensils for households and Sikh Gurdwaras' langar.

nodes.label: Nauroz / Nowruz (UNESCO ICH, 2016 multinational)
nodes.detail: Persian New Year marking spring equinox. India joined 7-country (now 12) multinational UNESCO ICH inscription 2016 (originally inscribed 2009). Celebrated by Parsis and Kashmiri communities in India. Cultural links to Zoroastrian tradition.

nodes.label: Yoga (UNESCO ICH, 2016)
nodes.detail: Physical, mental, spiritual practices of ancient Indian origin. UNESCO ICH Representative List 1 December 2016. UN declared 21 June International Day of Yoga (2014, observed from 2015). India's diplomatic outreach under PM Modi.

nodes.label: Kumbh Mela (UNESCO ICH, 2017)
nodes.detail: World's largest religious gathering. UNESCO ICH Representative List December 2017. Held every 12 years at 4 sites: Prayagraj (Ganga-Yamuna-Saraswati sangam), Haridwar, Nashik, Ujjain. Ardh Kumbh every 6 years. Prayagraj 2019 drew ~24 crore pilgrims; 2025 Mahakumbh ~66+ crore.

nodes.label: Durga Puja in Kolkata (UNESCO ICH, 2021)
nodes.detail: Annual festival of Durga worship in Kolkata, West Bengal. Inscribed UNESCO ICH Representative List 15 December 2021. Features elaborate pandals, artistic clay idols (kumartuli), community involvement spanning religions and classes. Immersion in Hooghly on Vijaya Dashami.

nodes.label: Garba of Gujarat (UNESCO ICH, 2023)
nodes.detail: Traditional folk dance of Gujarat performed during Navratri honouring Goddess Amba. UNESCO ICH Representative List 6 December 2023. Circular formation around a central garbi (lamp) or image. Accompanied by dholak, cymbals, songs. Popularised globally via Gujarati diaspora.

nodes.label: Qutb Minar & Monuments UNESCO Site (1993)
nodes.detail: Qutb Minar complex in Delhi inscribed UNESCO World Heritage Site 1993. 73m tall minaret built by Qutb-ud-din Aibak (1199 onwards). Includes Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque, Alai Darwaza, Iron Pillar of Delhi. Iconic of Delhi Sultanate architecture.

nodes.label: Humayun's Tomb UNESCO Site (1993)
nodes.detail: Mughal garden tomb of Emperor Humayun in Delhi, commissioned by his widow Bega Begum 1565, completed 1572. Architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyath. UNESCO WHS 1993. Precursor to Taj Mahal in charbagh garden plan. Aga Khan Trust restoration 2003-2013.

nodes.label: Darjeeling Himalayan Railway UNESCO Site (1999)
nodes.detail: Narrow-gauge mountain railway (1881) between Siliguri and Darjeeling, West Bengal. Inscribed UNESCO WHS 1999. Extended to include Nilgiri Mountain Railway (2005) and Kalka-Shimla Railway (2008) as 'Mountain Railways of India' serial site.

nodes.label: Bhimbetka Rock Shelters UNESCO Site (2003)
nodes.detail: Paleolithic-to-Medieval rock shelters near Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh with prehistoric paintings dating back ~30,000 years (Upper Palaeolithic to Historic). Discovered by V.S. Wakankar 1957. Inscribed UNESCO WHS 2003. 750+ shelters, 400+ with paintings across 7 hills.

nodes.label: Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus UNESCO Site (2004)
nodes.detail: Victorian Gothic railway station in Mumbai (originally Victoria Terminus), designed by F.W. Stevens 1878-87. Inscribed UNESCO WHS 2004. Blend of Victorian-Italianate Gothic and traditional Indian architecture.

nodes.label: Red Fort Complex UNESCO Site (2007)
nodes.detail: Mughal fortress-palace in Delhi built by Shah Jahan 1639-48 as capital of Shahjahanabad. UNESCO WHS 2007. PM's Independence Day address from Lahori Gate. Diwan-i-Aam, Diwan-i-Khas, Rang Mahal, Moti Masjid. Looted during 1857 revolt, again during British colonial period.

nodes.label: Jantar Mantar Jaipur UNESCO Site (2010)
nodes.detail: Astronomical observatory in Jaipur built by Sawai Jai Singh II, 1727-33. UNESCO WHS 2010. 19 monumental masonry instruments including the world's largest stone sundial. Delhi, Varanasi, Ujjain, Mathura also have Jantar Mantars.

nodes.label: Western Ghats UNESCO Site (2012)
nodes.detail: Serial natural WHS, inscribed 2012. 39 component sites across Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Maharashtra. One of 8 'hottest biodiversity hotspots' globally — 325 globally threatened species. Older than Himalayas. Part of UNESCO World Heritage List (Natural Criteria).

nodes.label: Hill Forts of Rajasthan UNESCO Site (2013)
nodes.detail: Serial WHS of 6 hill forts: Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh, Ranthambore, Amber, Jaisalmer, Gagron. Inscribed 2013. Examples of Rajput military architecture across 8th-19th centuries.

nodes.label: Rani ki Vav UNESCO Site (2014)
nodes.detail: 11th-century stepwell in Patan, Gujarat, built by Queen Udayamati in memory of Solanki king Bhimdev I (c.1063). Inscribed UNESCO WHS 2014. 7 storeys, 500+ sculptures depicting Hindu mythology. Featured on Rs 100 note.

nodes.label: Nalanda Mahavihara UNESCO Site (2016)
nodes.detail: Archaeological remains of ancient Buddhist mahavihara (monastic university), Bihar. Flourished 5th-12th centuries under Guptas and Palas. Inscribed UNESCO WHS 2016. Destroyed by Bakhtiyar Khilji c.1193. Modern Nalanda University established 2010.

nodes.label: Chandigarh Capitol (Le Corbusier) UNESCO Site (2016)
nodes.detail: Part of transnational serial WHS 'Architectural Work of Le Corbusier' inscribed 2016 across 7 countries. Indian component: Capitol Complex Chandigarh — Assembly, Secretariat, High Court (1950s-60s). Reflects modern movement architecture.

nodes.label: Historic City of Ahmadabad UNESCO Site (2017)
nodes.detail: Walled city founded by Sultan Ahmad Shah I 1411 on east bank of Sabarmati. Inscribed UNESCO WHS 8 July 2017 — first Indian city on the list. Heritage: pols (neighbourhoods), Jama Masjid, Sidi Saiyyed Jali, Sabarmati Ashram.

nodes.label: Jaipur City UNESCO Site (2019)
nodes.detail: Planned city founded by Sawai Jai Singh II 1727. Inscribed UNESCO WHS 2019 — second Indian city. Planned on Vedic architectural grid (9-square). Pink colour-washed 1876 in honour of Prince Albert's visit. Heritage: Hawa Mahal, City Palace, Jantar Mantar.

nodes.label: Kakatiya Rudreshwara (Ramappa) Temple UNESCO Site (2021)
nodes.detail: 13th-century Kakatiya-era Shaiva temple in Palampet, Telangana, built by Recharla Rudra under Kakatiya Ganapati Deva, 1213 CE. Sculptor Ramappa. UNESCO WHS 25 July 2021. Notable for sandbox foundation and lightweight floating bricks.

nodes.label: Dholavira UNESCO Site (2021)
nodes.detail: Harappan (Indus Valley) city in Kutch, Gujarat. Excavated by R.S. Bisht 1989-2005. UNESCO WHS 27 July 2021 — 40th Indian site. Three subdivisions (citadel/middle/lower town), sophisticated water management with 16 reservoirs. Dated 3000-1500 BCE.

nodes.label: Santiniketan UNESCO Site (2023)
nodes.detail: Educational and cultural centre founded by Rabindranath Tagore 1901, West Bengal. Inscribed UNESCO WHS 17 September 2023. Visva-Bharati University (1921). Pedagogy of nature-based education. Tagore's 'universalism' philosophy embodied in campus architecture.

nodes.label: Sacred Ensembles of Hoysalas UNESCO Site (2023)
nodes.detail: 12th-13th century Hoysala-era temples in Karnataka: Chennakeshava Temple (Belur), Hoysaleswara Temple (Halebidu), Keshava Temple (Somanathapura). UNESCO WHS 18 September 2023. Known for intricate stone carvings, star-shaped plans.

nodes.label: Charaideo Moidams UNESCO Site (2024)
nodes.detail: Ahom dynasty burial mounds (moidams) of Assam, built over 600 years (13th-19th centuries) at Charaideo. UNESCO WHS 2024 — first cultural site from North-East India. 90 moidams at site; vaulted underground chambers.

nodes.label: Geographical Indications Act 1999
nodes.detail: Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act 1999, in force 15 September 2003. Implements TRIPS GI obligation. GI Registry in Chennai. First GI: Darjeeling Tea (2004). 600+ GIs registered by 2024 including Basmati, Mysore Silk, Kanchipuram Saree, Banarasi Saree, Banaganapalle Mangoes.

nodes.label: National Culture Fund (1996)
nodes.detail: Public charitable trust set up under Charitable Endowments Act 1890, registered 28 November 1996. Enables private sector and individuals to partner in conservation/promotion of India's cultural heritage. CSR contributions eligible. Major projects: Humayun's Tomb restoration, Qutub Minar complex.

nodes.label: International Day of Yoga (21 June, UN 2014)
nodes.detail: Proposed by PM Modi at UNGA 27 September 2014. Adopted unanimously by UNGA 11 December 2014 (177 co-sponsors). First observed 21 June 2015. Marks summer solstice (longest day). Common Yoga Protocol performed. India's soft-power diplomacy success.

nodes.label: Chandrayaan-1 Lunar Mission (2008)
nodes.detail: India's first lunar probe, launched 22 October 2008 by PSLV-C11 from Sriharikota. Operational phase November 2008 - August 2009. Major discovery: water molecules on Moon (September 2009, with NASA M3 instrument). Mission cost Rs 386 crore. Established India as 6th country to reach Moon.

nodes.label: Mangalyaan / Mars Orbiter Mission (2013)
nodes.detail: India's first interplanetary mission, launched 5 November 2013 by PSLV-C25. Achieved Mars orbit 24 September 2014. First Asian nation, fourth space agency to reach Mars. First nation to succeed in first Mars attempt. Cost Rs 450 crore — lower than Hollywood film Gravity. Operational till April 2022.

nodes.label: Chandrayaan-2 Mission (2019)
nodes.detail: India's second lunar mission, launched 22 July 2019 by GSLV Mk-III. Orbiter-Lander-Rover (Vikram-Pragyan). Lander crash-landed 7 September 2019 near south pole. Orbiter continues operations. Terrain Mapping Camera, Dual-Frequency Synthetic Aperture Radar instruments.

nodes.label: Chandrayaan-3 Soft Landing (23 August 2023)
nodes.detail: India's third lunar mission, launched 14 July 2023 by LVM3 Mk-III. Soft-landed Vikram lander + Pragyan rover near Moon's south pole, 23 August 2023 — first country to achieve south pole soft-landing; 4th to soft-land on Moon. National Space Day 23 August instituted. Confirmed presence of elements (Al, Ca, Fe, S, Ti) near south pole.

nodes.label: Aditya-L1 Solar Mission (2023)
nodes.detail: India's first solar observation mission, launched 2 September 2023 by PSLV-C57. Placed in halo orbit around Sun-Earth L1 Lagrangian point (~1.5 million km) on 6 January 2024. 7 payloads to study solar corona, chromosphere, solar wind.

nodes.label: National Quantum Mission (2023)
nodes.detail: Approved by Union Cabinet 19 April 2023. Rs 6,003 crore outlay (2023-31). Targets: develop quantum computers (50-1000 physical qubits), quantum communication, quantum sensing, quantum materials. DST nodal. 4 T-Hubs at IIT Bombay, IISc, IIT Madras, IIT Delhi.

nodes.label: Gaganyaan (Indian Human Spaceflight Programme)
nodes.detail: India's human spaceflight programme, announced 15 August 2018 by PM Modi. First crewed mission targeted 2026. Test flights: Gaganyaan-1 (uncrewed, TV-D1 test October 2023), G-1, G-2 before crewed G-3. 3-member crew, LEO mission. Budget Rs 10,000+ crore expanded to Rs 20,000 crore.

nodes.label: Shankar Dayal Sharma (President 1992-97)
nodes.detail: 9th President of India (25 July 1992 - 25 July 1997). Former Vice President (1987-92). Imposed President's Rule on BJP state governments after Babri demolition. Oversaw coalition governments' swearing-in (Narasimha Rao, Deve Gowda).

nodes.label: K.R. Narayanan (President 1997-2002)
nodes.detail: 10th President of India (25 July 1997 - 25 July 2002). First Dalit President. Dismissed Gujarat government's advice on President's Rule 1998. Broke convention by publicly warning PM during Gujarat 2002 riots. Former diplomat, VP.

nodes.label: A.P.J. Abdul Kalam (President 2002-07)
nodes.detail: 11th President of India (25 July 2002 - 25 July 2007). Eminent aerospace scientist, 'Missile Man of India'. Led Pokhran-II team as DRDO head. Authored 'Wings of Fire', 'India 2020'. Died 27 July 2015. Bharat Ratna 1997.
